author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have read with interest the details of the ceremonies which took place at Vienna. I desire you to appoint a committee to examine if the ceremonial was in conformity with that followed on previous occasions, […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I do not consider it right that you should issue a proclamation to your people. Simply send a message to the legislative body, which must not be printed, saying that the independence of Holland can exist only as long as it is not incompatible with the interests of France; […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Caulaincourt has informed me of all the amiable things which your Majesty has said on the subject of my marriage. I beg you to accept my thanks. My feelings towards you are as unchangeable as the political principles which govern the relations of my empire. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Prince Kourakine has handed me the letter which your Majesty has been good enough to write in order to congratulate me on my marriage. This minister of state has equally expressed to me, on the part of your Majesty, your good wishes for my happiness and for that of the Empress, […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “You will receive from the office of the secretary of state a decree annulling that which appointed Fouche to the government of Rome. Inform General Miollis that it is my intention to leave him at the post which he fulfils so well, and that I reckon upon his zeal. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Sir, my Brother and very dear Father-in-law,— I have received the letter of your Imperial Majesty of the 15th. I beg you to receive my thanks for the amiable things which it contains. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I cannot allow Prince Kourakine to leave without reiterating to him my feelings towards your Imperial Majesty. Those which I bear your Majesty, as well as the political considerations of my empire, […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain
context: Duchy of Warsaw arms: explained away.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Exactions of all kinds are committed in Spain, and a traffic is made of the liberation of prisoners. Send an officer with a letter to General Kellermann. Write at the same time to Massena to have the individuals guilty of these crimes arrested. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “On Sunday I shall hold a parade in Paris, at which will be present the Portuguese legion quartered at Meaux, a battalion of the rear guard of the army of Spain, the Dutch Guard, and my French Guard. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I beg that you will continue to take measures for procuring me all the works published in England, either concerning my policy or on the affairs of the day. I derive very important intelligence from them. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Send Madame Mere a passport for King Louis by which he will be able to go to any part of the south of France or of Italy, and to reside there. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Reply to General Belliard,2 that you have laid his letter before me; that he must have lost his head when he wrote it; that to offer his resignation on account of not obeying orders is equivalent to declaring that he will not obey; that this is to incur the penalty of capital punishment; […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain
context: Germany garrisoned for the coming war.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I send you extracts from the English journals. You must show them to Prince Kourakine while conversing with him. After this you must send them to Comte Lauriston, so that he may show them in Russia. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Which is the best port for assembling my squadron of the ocean? I see only two between which to choose — Brest or Cherbourg. Which of those two ports offers the greatest facilities for invading England or Ireland? Which of the two offers the greatest facilities for sailing to America and India?. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain
context: The navy in the northern scheme.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The Boulogne flotilla has returned to harbour. It sustained some damage. I think even that a gunboat went down. Write that this should cause no discouragement. These gales are just the things to exercise the crews. " Napoleon.'* To marshal berthier. "St. Cloud, 13rd August, 1811. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I beg that you will have the fortifications of Geneva blown up. Perhaps in a military point of view it would be of interest to keep this place; but, the inhabitants having always exhibited a bad feeling, I have decided upon blowing up the fortifications without delay. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I beg that you will pay 2,500 francs a month to the ex-Queen of Etruria, at her convent in Rome. The poor Queen of Etruria, deprived of her kingdom, which was handed over by Napoleon to his sister Eliza, was most cruelly treated. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have received your letter concerning the cheating of Bourrienne at Hamburg. It will be important to throw light upon what he has done. Have the Jew, Gumprecht Mares, arrested, seize his papers, and place him in solitary confinement. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I return you the letters from Savona. Reply yourself to the Doctor Porta that you have laid his letter before the Emperor; that his Majesty has written in the margin of his letter from Amsterdam that no matter what discussions may have taken place between the Pope and his Majesty, […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have just seen the porcelain service sent to the Empress as a new year's gift. It is very ugly. See that it be prettier another year. Have a breakfast service made, and on each cup the portraits of the Empress and of the six princesses, my sisters and sister-in-law. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “It will be necessary to send a courier to Comte Lauriston to-day. Do not speak to him about the espionage of Czernitchef, of which you are supposed to know nothing at present. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I return you the letters of your brother. Reply that cacao, sugar, and coffee are not English merchandise, and ought not to be burned. What ought to be burned are articles of English manufacture. But as there are. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Write to Marshal Ney that his corps is diverging from the route traced out for it, and commits devastation everywhere. And on the 20th June Berthier was told to write to Prince Schwartzenberg saying that as his funds had not. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Marshal Davoust had a battle on the 23rd at Mohilef; I have not yet learned the details. Bagration wished to.trample over him and was defeated. A note, written at six in the evening, on the field of battle, said that the enemy had been defeated. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Write to Marshal Ney that the situation of his army corps seems to me very alarming as regards his artillery. Without artillery his corps would be greatly compromised. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have received the portrait of the King, and find it very like him. It furnishes me with an opportunity, of which I avail myself with pleasure, of expressing my satisfaction with the care you take of him. To the EMPEROR OF AUSTRIA. " Smolensko, 242$ August, 1812. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain
context: Smolensk: news for the King of Rome's governess.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I beg that you will see if the two or three hundred carts left behind at Wilna, exposed to the air, have been placed under cover in a church or an arsenal. If that has not yet been done the governor should see to it. " Napoleon.". […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have received your Calculation of Probabilities with pleasure. There was a time when I should have read it with interest; to-day I must confine myself to expressing the satisfaction which I experience every time that I see you bring out new works. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “We have reached Viazma. The enemy continue their retreat upon Moscow. I am waiting for news as to the march of the 16th and 22nd Russian divisions, which are coming from Moldavia. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Reiterate the order to General Marchand to pick up all the sick and wounded at the abbey of Mojafsk, making use for this purpose of all the carriages and carts without distinction. Give orders to this effect to the staff. I have ordered my grand equerry to take at least 100 of my baggage-waggons. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have just passed the Beresina, but the ice floating down that river makes the bridges very unstable. The 87 army which was opposed to Schwartzenberg wished to dispute the passage; to-night it is concentrated on the right bank of the river at Borisoff. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I remain a moment at Dresden in order to write to your Majesty. In spite of great fatigue my health never was better. I started on the 4th. after the battle of Beresina, from Lithuania, leaving the Grand Army under the orders of the King of Naples. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have received your letter of the 2nd December. I see nothing very important in the Moniteur on the subject of Spain. The resistance of the castle of Burgos is a fine military affair, but it simply proves that forts are not to be taken without siege guns. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “You must go to Berlin, and before leaving Wilna let me know how things are looking. You will find at Berlin a letter for the King of Prussia, and my instructions for yourself. You must wait at Berlin for orders and write to me every day. " Napoleon." under arms, expecting to be attacked. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain
context: Smorgoni: command to Murat, sledge to Paris.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have received your letter of the 16th. I have already told you that I see the command of the army in your hands with pleasure. I find the conduct of the King of Naples very extravagant, and such that it would require very little for me to have him arrested by way of an example. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “All your efforts should tend towards preserving Warsaw. The reports which reach me from all sides show that the Russians on the Beresina thought themselves lost; […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have received your letter from Leipsic. As soon as you receive news of General Morand, let me know,. even the rumours which may reach you. By our latest news it appears still undecided whether Prussia will take the field against us. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “It is unfortunate with your intelligence that you will not see that Magdeburg can only be provisioned by means of requisitions, that these means are authorised by a state of war; that they have been constantly employed since the world was the world; […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I do not intend that you should transmit direct to the Empress your memoranda on police affairs. That can have no advantage and has many objections. The Empress is too young to have her mind corrupted or disturbed by police details. "Napoleon.”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Knowing the interest which your Majesty takes in every piece of good fortune which befalls to me, I hasten to announce the victory which it has pleased Providence to VOL. ill. R. grant to my arms in the field of Lutzen. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “We have arrived at Dresden; I am master of both banks and of the strong places on the Elbe. It is probable that I shall march into Silesia. After having been long in disgrace, and having nearly lost his head, Fouche now received the following letter: — "Dresden, 10th May, 1813. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I delivered battle to the Russian and Prussian army, intrenched in the camps of Bautzen and of Kochkirch, on the 20th and the 21st. Providence granted me the victory. I hasten to inform your Majesty that my health is excellent, counting upon the interest you bear me. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Send the inclosed letter to M. de Serra at Prague. " The Emperor has arrived at Dresden. To-morrow the army will pass the river in pursuit of the enemy Inclosed you will find a letter on the subject of the conduct of General Thielman. You must tell M. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The Swedish troops having entered Hamburg, it is right that you should at once send me a declaration of war against Sweden. " Napoleon.”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The question asked by General Csesar Berthier as to the conduct he should pursue with regard to Queen Caroline of Sicily is probably an idle one. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have seen with pleasure that amidst the vicissitudes of political events the feelings of your Majesty have remained unchangeable. The evil intentions of Sweden towards me are the result of my constant refusal to adhere to the spoliation of Norway. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The Bishop of Nantes was the most enlightened priest of the Empire, the most distinguished doctor of the Sorbonne; he can be placed alongside of the most honoured bishops of the Gallican Church. No one was more penetrated with the true spirit of the Gospel; no. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have long thought that Caulaincourt and de Narbonne allow themselves to be taken in by the honeyed style. Metternich. The stipulations between the Austrians and the Russians were agreed upon last February, […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have already informed you that Marshal Oudinot, together with General Vandamme, General Regnier, and the Due de Padoue (Arrighi), with an army of 80,000 men, will debouch by Luckau and Bayreuth the day the rupture of the armistice takes place, so as to be within three or four days of Berlin. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “It is necessary for you to present me a project for according gratifications to the actors of my theatre, and to inform the Comte de Turenne that he must, take measures to send the actors back to France on the 12th. " Napoleon." to prince cambaceres. "Dresden, gtk August, 1813. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The Minister of Foreign Affairs will have informed you that Austria has declared war. Her manifesto is insignificant enough. In plain French it simply comes to this, that she considers the opportunity a good one to recover her influence. " The negotiations of Prague did not take place. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I informed you of my intentions yesterday. The whole army of the enemy presented itself before Dresden yesterday, and Marshal St. Cyr feared that he would be attacked to-day; I am going there. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain
context: Kulm mission: cut the allies' rear.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The allied army, commanded by the Emperor Alexander, has been entirely defeated. I captured 30,000 men, 40 or 50 guns, 30 standards, &c. The enemy abandoned more than 12,000 wounded men in the villages. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Write thus to Marshal Ney — 'We have just received news from Marshal Oudinot who deemed fit to venture within two marches of Wittenberg. The result of this rash movement is that the corps of General Tauenstein and a strong body of Cossacks are interfering with the communications of Marshal Macdonald […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Marshal Macdonald is to-day at Gcerlitz. Should he continue his retrograde movement, it will be necessary for me to march to his assistance. The misfortune which has happened to the first corps is one which could not have been expected. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have arrived here. The Bavarians and Austrians, 60,000 strong, posted at Hanau, tried to cut me off from France. I gave them a good drubbing, and captured their guns, standards, and 6,000 prisoners. My health was never better. I am going to Mayence. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The movement of the English upon Bayonne has opened up a portion of the frontier. I learn that they have already landed a certain quantity of their merchandise near St. Jean-de-Luz. I suppose that you have removed your custom-house line. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Give orders that if ever the English arrive at the castle of Marracq (near Bayonne) it be set fire to; also to all the houses which belong to me, so that they may not sleep in my bed. « NAPOLEON." ST. JEAN-DE-LUZ. 283 To M. FOUCHE, at Bologna. "St. Cloud, i$th November, 1813. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “On the 27th I marched upon St. Dizier, which was occupied by the enemy. I drove them out, captured some guns, killed a few men, and took a few prisoners. I learned here that Blucher with 25,000 men had gone to Brienne, where he arrived to-day. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “You must leave garrisons in all the places, call in General Sebastiani and your cavalry, march upon. Meuse and manoeuvre on Blucher's right flank in the direction of Namur. " Marshal Marmont will manoeuvre round Metz. Marshals Ney and Victor will guard the passes of the Vosges. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “What! six hours after having received the first troops coming from Spain you were not in the field! Six hours' repose was sufficient. I won the action of Nangis with a brigade of dragoons coming from Spain, which, since it left Bayonne, had not unbridled its horses. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “It seems that the allies have selected the 3rd February for the opening of the Congress at Chatillon; that Lord Cathcart will treat for England with a dozen Englishmen, Stadion for Austria, Humbolt for Prussia, and Razoumosky for Russia. I shall be to-morrow at Troyes. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I am much surprised that Marshal Suchet should not have despatched the troops which I demanded from Lyons. They ought to have arrived and I hear no more of them. If the marshal has taked upon himself not to execute orders he is very culpable. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have just arrived at Nogent. The enemy after Montereau fell back upon Troyes with the greater portion of their army. They enjoyed great luck, for the frost enabled them to march across country; but for this half their baggage and their artillery would have been captured. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I send you a line to let you know the happy issue of the battle of Vauchamps. General Blucher, who was separated from his army, and who had his head-quarters at Vertus, had been joined by Kleist's corps, twentyfour battalions strong, and by a new Russian corps of twelve battalions, or 20,000 men. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I see with pleasure the advantages which you have obtained; if they had been a little more decisive we should have been able to keep Italy. I have destroyed the army of Silesia, composed of Russians and Prussians. I began yesterday to beat Schwartzenberg. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The Due de Bassano (M. Maret) will send you a copy of the proposals of the allies. You will see by them that your sermons are out of place, and that I do not require to be preached to in order to sign an honourable peace if that be possible. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Before commencing the fortifications of Paris the plan must be known, that which has been presented to me appears to be very complicated; more simplicity is required. " I receive complaints from all quarters against the mayors and the bourgeois, who prevent the people from defending themselves. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have arrived at Rheims, which General St. Priest had occupied with three Russian divisions and a Prussian division which had just arrived from Stettin. I beat them; I retook the town, 20 guns, a great deal of baggage, and. made 5,000 prisoners. General St. Priest was mortally wounded. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Marshal Mortier writes that — ■' The enemy are in full retreat, and seem to be falling back upon Laon. I have sent some cavalry to follow their march, which is being made in good order.'. Send some peasants to try and find out if the enemy are in force at Craonne. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The army which I beat at Craonne was the Russian army. It lost heavily, and fell back upon Laon, where it was joined by the corps of Bulow, York, and Kleist, forming the Prussian army. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Yesterday I crossed the Aube at Plancy, and at once marched upon Mery. I attacked the town, which was carried at 7 P.M. The Emperor Alexander was at Arcis on the 18th. He remained there only a hour; we were nearly face to face. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Send a gendarme in disguise to Metz, one to Bar, and another to Nancy, with letters to the mayors. Tell them that we are marching on the rear of the enemy; […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “It is my intention to appoint the mayor of Porto Longone commandant of my palace at Porto Longone. He must perform the functions of commandant, concierge, keeper of the robes, and overseer of the gardens. He will receive a salary of 600 francs. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I think that I asked you to write to the Princess Pauline not to bring her piano master with her, but only a good singer and a good songstress, seeing that we have here a good violin player and a good pianist. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Write to the Princess Pauline that I have received all the letters from Naples; tell her that I feel much hurt that my letters should have been forwarded open, as if I were a prisoner; that I find this conduct ridiculous and insulting., " Napoleon." to general bertrand. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I am leaving the island of Elba. I have been extremely satisfied with the conduct of the inhabitants. I confide to them the safety of this country, to which I attach a great importance. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain
context: Farewell to Elba: embarking for France.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Send me a plan for enabling Soissons, La Fere, and Chateau Thierry to resist a sudden attack. It appears that the Due d'Angouleme was at Avignon on the 23rd I suppose that events in Paris made him feel the necessity of falling back. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain
context: Soissons, La Fère, Château-Thierry to resist attack.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “You must efface Berthier, Marmont, Victor, Perignon, Augereau, and Kellermann from the list of marshals. You must present me a report, so that a pension may be granted to those marshals who have no fortune. To COMTE MOLLIEN {Minister of the Treasury). "Paris, \\th April, 1815. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain
context: Efface Berthier, Marmont, Victor and the rest from the marshals' list.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “It would be well to order in each department the fabrication of a certain number of pikes. Select a model. They will be of use in default of muskets and scythes. " Napoleon.”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain
context: Pikes in every department, against musket shortage.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Tell Marshal Suchet, if he is still at Lyons, to remain there, and if he has left send him a courier, so that he may return. I give the command of the army of •■ the" Alps definitively to that marshal. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I approve of Marshal Soult receiving a salary of 40,000 francs as Marshal of the Empire, and 40,000 francs as General-in-Chief. I approve of him receiving 6,000 francs a month for staff and office expenses, and 20,000 francs for travelling, […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “It is probable that the Guard will soon march; there will then remain no troops in Paris. It is important that by the 1st June, at the latest, the quartermaster-generals, colonels, majors, captains, &c, of the National Guard should receive their commissions. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain
context: Guard soon marching; Paris quarters must be ready.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Enclosed you will find a copy of the orders which I have given for the cavalry of the army. Marshal Grouchy will command it in chief. Give him a chief of the staff, and a general of artillery. All the generals on the unattached list are at his service. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain
context: Grouchy gets the cavalry; Suchet takes Montmélian.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Give orders so that there may be at least 200 guns in position at the different gates and in the works round. Paris by the 12th June. Let me know when the first naval guns will arrive. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain
context: 200 guns at Paris gates and works.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “FRENCHMEN, — The defection of Marshal Augereau delivered Lyons, without defence, to our enemies. The army which I confided to him was strong enough to. the Austrians, and to fall upon the rear of the left wing of the army which threatened Paris. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The bulletin will have acquainted you with what happened yesterday. I am going to transfer my headquarters to Fleurus. We are executing a movement on a large scale. I greatly regret the loss of General Letort. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I send you my aide-de-camp, General Flahault, with the present letter. I wish to write to you in detail because it is of the greatest importance. " Marshal Grouchy is marching on Sombreffe with the third and fourth eorps of infantry. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain
context: Fateful orders: Grouchy to Sombreffe, Guard to Fleurus; Brussels the prize.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I am going to transfer my imperial head-quarters this evening to Beaumont. To-morrow, the 15th, I shall move to Charleroi, where the Prussian army is; this will give rise to a battle or to the retreat of the enemy. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain
context: Beaumont headquarters; Charleroi tomorrow. Dateline corrected from content.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “SOLDIERS, — In yielding tp the necessity which obliges me to quit the brave French army, I carry away with me the happy certainty that it will justify, by the eminent services, which the country expects from it, the praises which even our enemies cannot refuse. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Borodino Sept. 7, 181 2. " Soldiers: This is the battle you have so much desired. The victory depends upon you! It is now necessary to us. It will give us abundance of good winter quarters, and a prompt return to our country. […]”

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Alexander I., Emperor of Russia. Moscow, Sept. 20, 181 2. " Monsieur, my brother: — Having been informed that the brother of your Imperial Majesty's Minister at Cassel was in Moscow, I sent for him, and we have had a conversation of some length. I have advised his making my sentiments known to your Majesty. […]”

displayText: “only obstacle to the reestablishment of peace in Europe, the Emperor Napoleon, faithful to his oath, declares that he is ready to descend from the throne, to leave Europe, and even to lay down his life for the welfare of his country, which is inseparable from the rights of his son, those of the regency of the Empress, […]”

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Old Guards April 20, 18 14. " Soldiers of my old guard, I bid you farewell. For twenty years I have constantly accompanied you on the road to honor and glory. In these latter times, as in the days of our prosperity, you have invariably been models of courage and fidelity. […]”

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Marengo and Friedland fime 14, 181 j. " Soldiers: This day is the anniversary of Marengo and Friedland, which twice decided the destiny of Europe. Then, as after the battles of Austerlitz and Wagram, we were too generous. We believed in the protestations and oaths of princes to whom we left their thrones. […]”

context: Are we not still the same men?

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Belgians, the Hanoverians, the soldiers of the Confederation of the Rhine, lament that they are obliged to use their arms in the cause of princes who are the enemies of justice, and the destroyers of the rights of nations. They well know the coalition to be insatiable. […]”

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Bellerophon; I am not a prisoner; I am the guest of England. I was, indeed, instigated to come on board by the captain, who told me that he had been directed by his Government to receive me and my suite, and conduct me to England, if agreeable to my wishes. […]”
archive: Tarbell, Napoleon's Addresses (1897) — public domain translations

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My love — D'Audenarde, whom I sent to you this morning, informs me that you have no more fortitude since you have 12 been at Malmaison. And yet that place is full of our affection which will not and can not ever change, at least on my part. […]”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My love — I have received your letter of the 19th of April. It is in a bad style. I am always the same. My affections never change. I know not what Eugene may have said to you. […]”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have received your letter. I see with pain the danger through which you have passed. For an inhabitant of the isles of the ocean to perish in a lake — that had been a fatality. The queen is better, and I hope that her health will soon be restored. […]”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have received, my love, your letter of the 14th of July. I see with pleasure that the waters have done you good, and that you like Geneva. I think that you will do well to remain there several weeks. My health is pretty good. The conduct of the King of Holland grieves me. […]”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My love — I have received your letter of the 9th of September. I learn with pleasure that you are well. The Empress is decidedly enciente for four months. She is well and is very much attached to me. The little Princes Napoleon are very well. They are at the Italian pavilion in the park of St. […]”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have received your letter. Hortense, whom I have seen, will tell you what I think. Go to see your son this winter; return the next year to the waters of Aix, or spend the spring time at Navarre. I should advise you to go immediately to Navarre did I not fear that you would be lonely. […]”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My love — I have received your letter. Hortense has spoken to me of you. I see with pleasure that you are contented. I 1 "Hortense was a woman of very superior accomplishments. […]”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have received your letter for the new year. I thank you for what you say to me. I see with pleasure that you are contented. They say that at Navarre there are more ladies than gentlemen. My health is very good, though I have not been out for a fortnight. […]”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My love — I have received your letter. I thank you. My son is stout and very well. I hope that he will be prospered, qu'il viendra a bien. He has my chest, my mouth, and eyes. I hope that he will fulfill his destiny. I am always well pleased with Eugene. He has never caused me any dissatisfaction. […]”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain
context: My son is stout: the King of Rome thrives.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have received your letter. I see with pleasure that you are in good health. I have been some days at Trianon.
